transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

Thank you. Well, I came in because my sleep has really become a problem. I’m usually a very disciplined sleeper, but... since my cousin died, I just lie awake replaying that night. And when I do manage to drift off, I end up waking up at 3 or 4 in the morning from these scraps of hospital images in my head. Then I have to go into board meetings feeling like I’ve only slept in pieces. It's just not sustainable for me.
How long ago did your cousin pass away?
It's been about three weeks. That's when she died in the highway collision. So, this whole sleep issue has been going on since then.

Besides the sleep problems and the images from the hospital, have you been having unwanted thoughts about that night that pop into your head during the day, even when you're trying to focus on other things?

Yes, I have. It happens at odd moments, really. Um, especially if I hear a phone ring late, or if I'm driving and see the glare of headlights on the highway. 

When that happens, a very sharp picture of the hospital corridor just pushes into my mind, or I'll suddenly hear the police officer’s voice again. I usually just have to take a moment and pause to steady myself before I can get back to what I was doing.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F43.12 (Prolonged Depressive Reaction) and F51.02 (Insomnia due to mental disorder) as primary diagnoses. Patient presents with classic acute stress disorder symptoms: intrusive memories/flashbacks triggered by reminders, sleep disturbance with nightmares, hyperarousal to trauma cues (phone rings, headlights), and onset within 3 weeks of traumatic event. F43.10 (Acute Stress Disorder) is the clear match.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient meets diagnostic criteria for Post-traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), Acute phase. The patient experienced a qualifying traumatic stressor (cousin's death in highway collision 3 weeks ago), with confirmed intrusive symptoms (unwanted thoughts, flashbacks triggered by reminders like phone rings and headlights), nightmares with hospital imagery, and sleep disturbance. Symptoms began immediately after the traumatic event and persist within the 3-month window for acute PTSD. Functional impairment is evident in work performance during board meetings.
